Row.Text: As the Roman Empire widens its sprawl, those living at its heart grow greedy and complacent. Roads crumble as pockets sag heavier with coin skimmed from tax revenue, and many elites see no further than besting their political rivals. Administration has turned from a sacred duty to a comfortable sinecure, while the Roman people starve and the once-renowned infrastructure of the Empire’s peak rots.
A restored cursus honorum can bring Rome forward into the future.
In the army is Rome’s strength.

Egypt is the kingdom that, like the Nile, might rise and fall but never vanishes. But every river needs a spring. The rule of god-kings grows less and less effective as empires become bureaucracies, and it is good accounting, not divine favor, that fills granaries and funds irrigation teams.
Egypt will pass through the night-lands and fear not the Apophis-serpent. The pharaoh will have their functionaries.
Egypt is the land of the sun. One does not assign an administrative assistant to the sun.

The sons and daughters of the merchant class parade through the Aksumite square, dressed in silk shamma and fine linen kemis - finer than any noble-born child could afford. In the court, the nobility clamors for sumptuary laws, prohibiting commoners from parading in such finery.
Money runs Aksum, not the carvings on stelae. Back the merchants.
Aksum is nothing without its soul. Back the nobles.

The philosophers of Greece have their works translated, analyzed, elaborated upon, and often plagiarized. Greek words enter foreign vocabularies, Greek concepts are taken up as the foundations of thought in places far from Greek soil. But the thinkers remembered are thinkers from the past – present-day Greece remains an afterthought. Even as its past glories are remembered, its influence wanes.
Greek thinkers continue to think. Greek ideas continue to develop. The Hellenistic world still lives.
The ancient world of logios and hoplite is a distant land for present-day Greeks as well.

Han expands outward into the world: not to explore and catalog newness, but to bring the world under a common rationality. A common set of standards, a universal listing of names and terms - these further scientific inquiry, but risk conflict with those who think differently.
Standardization, metrics, centralization. This is the only way forward
Han must relax its terms to achieve its goals.

Each year, the rains bring fresh life to the Khmer. Each year, the population drinks the reservoirs dry. One bad drought could spell disaster. The tasks of dredging old baray and cutting new, reinforced canals must be done, but they are hardly glorious jobs.
No one’s name will be inscribed on stelae. No king’s face will grace a stupa. Workers will dig, and water will flow.

In the Maurya street, one hears hundreds of languages; there are shrines to scores of gods; a thousand different styles of dress. But the umbrella of Maurya rule - the chhatra - can only extend so far, and the world now seems almost incomprehensibly vast. Bureaucrats balancing the demands of groups against groups develop headaches.
Expand the chhatra. All are Maurya.

Maya travelers have moved far from their former homeland, and have seen many strange sights. For instance, the length of day, the track of ‘K’iinich Ahau in the sky, and the rising of Kukulkan seem different when one is far from home. Maya settlements wonder what might it mean to live under different stars and different suns.
It means different people and different rites. Bring forth the poet-priests.
It means different futures and fortunes. Bring forth the mathematician-astrologers.

When a noble of the Mississippians dies, they are buried with beads, weapons, and all the symbols of status – including scores of servants, strangled and laid in graves. As new technologies and connections make for more prosperous nobles, the size of these graves have increased – as have the numbers of furious commoners who have lost a relative to serve the nobles in the next world.
Nobles need to be served in the next life as in this one. But perhaps one can sacrifice a name and title, not a body.
Times change. So do the Mississippian noble privileges.

Achamaenid rule is fractal – the power of the glorious center is repeated in miniature form on its fringes. But as the center grows, a problem arises: local rulers are caught between enacting their own shah-dom and petitioning for a role in the glorious court at {1_Capital}. Local rulers return after years in the capital to find lands that no longer recognize their authority. Assassinations become fashionable.
Keep rule as it is – each lesser fire a reflection of the central fire. Persia will adapt, but remain Achamaenid.

Just beyond the edges of America, there are strange figures that live beyond settled lands. They are called “mountain men,” though not all of them live in the mountains, and not all of them are men. But they are Americans who have decided that they will not be constrained by borders or convention.
They might be a source of information on matters abroad.
They might be a source of income (so long as customs agents do not ask questions).

Pride and prestige are the currency on which feudal kingdoms grow. Ganda have cultivated a reputation for courtesy and civility… so much that Ganda emissaries are allowed to travel wherever they see fit.
Courtesy is a two-way street. Ganda emissaries are worthy of trust.
Ganda wanderers can also scout for new opportunities. In their off-hours, of course.

The maior palatii - the chief steward - of {1_Capital} has been too generous. Nobility have the right to hand out titles as they see fit, but upon naming his personal chef a barony (and seeing the cook parade about in noble colors), people have begun to talk.
Nobility should be tied to land, not favor.

The messenger rides as swiftly as he can carrying orders: provincial engineers and construction crews are needed to fortify embankments. Upon arriving, though, everyone has gone: the local daimyo already issued orders.
This is the kind of flexibility Meiji needs; local leaders know best.
The Meiji center holds the larger picture, and can act with greater foresight than some local lord.

A Mexican municipal organization - a calbido - has attracted attention: all may serve in high positions regardless of their birth status. Foreigners, indigenous, and even former servants vie for high office on the basis of their words and deeds. Not all are pleased.
Farmers’ taxes are paid as a share of whatever they have produced. But this year’s yield has just been awkward: goats, goats, and more goats, and the empire needed iron.
This sounds like a problem of distribution. Get those goats where they can be of use.
Reform taxes - all taxes are to be paid in silver. Please, no more goats.

If there is one hero that Prussians love to hear about, it is the knight. Two stories circulate, seemingly endlessly: the pious and chivalric Parzival, who quests for holiness and flees sin; and Sigfried and the winning of a dragon’s hoard.
That dragon sounds like it would make for a good illustration.

Qing society is a carefully orchestrated structure - cohong govern trade, banners govern war. When a new society is conquered, it is not repressed, but brought within this system. Provided that the newcomers know their place.
The cohong are key here to ensure that goods and money circulate.
The banners are key here to ensure peace.

The herbalist’s donkey gives a grunt of annoyance as the herbalist loads her lechebniki - her books of herb-lore - onto its back. The books are heavy, yes, but they are valuable not only for the hours of work put into inscribing them, but also for their potential.
Supplement these traveling collections with stories of the saints.
Perhaps she should have a set place where she might practice her art.

The dwellers in the hills and mountains have always been just outside of Siamese society. But their people are not strangers: silver and cowrie-adorned women carry forest goods to market before dawn each morning. Now, their fierce, tiger-hunting chief seeks an agreement of peace between the mountain people and the Siamese.
Sign it on palm-leaf, with a stylus. Like civilized people do.
Break a buffalo skull in two, that each side might keep a horn to remember the promise, as his people do.

After extensive travel, Dr Rizal seeks a quiet moment to himself. He reflects on all he has observed in {1_SUBJECT_CIVILIZATION_ADJ} lands, opening his notebook to a blank page. What he writes, he will remember of this place for all time.
